title: US Wait Times for Cancer Surgery Are Growing Longer, New Study Finds
excerpt: A large-scale analysis shows American cancer patients are waiting significantly longer between diagnosis and surgery, with delays linked to worse survival outcomes across multiple cancer types.
body:
• Wait times between cancer diagnosis and surgery in the US have increased steadily over the past two decades, according to a new study.
  • Delays beyond four to six weeks are associated with measurably worse survival outcomes across several common cancer types, including breast, lung, and colorectal cancers.
  • Black and Hispanic patients, those with Medicaid or no insurance, and patients in rural areas face the longest wait times.
  • Researchers say the findings underscore the need for systemic changes to reduce treatment delays, particularly as cancer diagnoses rise with an aging population.

A Widening Gap Between Diagnosis and Treatment

American cancer patients are waiting longer than ever to reach the operating room, according to a study drawing attention across the medical community. The research, which analyzed large national datasets, found that the median time between cancer diagnosis and initial surgical treatment has increased significantly over the past two decades — a trend that accelerated during and after the COVID-19 pandemic.

The delays are not evenly distributed. Patients in rural areas, those on Medicaid or without insurance, and Black and Hispanic patients consistently face the longest waits. For some, the gap between diagnosis and surgery stretches well past the thresholds that research links to worse outcomes.

Every Week of Delay Carries a Cost

The clinical stakes of surgical delay are well established. Prior research published in journals including JAMA Network Open and The BMJ has shown that for breast cancer, a delay of six weeks or more is associated with exponentially higher mortality risk. For lung cancer, patients who wait more than 12 weeks for surgery face a significantly higher risk of recurrence and death. A 2020 meta-analysis in The BMJ found that a four-week delay in treatment was associated with a 6-8% increase in the risk of death for surgical cancers.

"The longer patients wait, the more opportunity there is for cancer to progress. Every effort to reduce system-level delays could improve population-level survival."

— Researchers, cancer treatment delay study

Structural Barriers Drive the Problem

Researchers point to several forces behind the lengthening waits. The supply of surgical capacity has not kept pace with demand from a growing and aging population. More complex diagnostic workups — including advanced imaging, genetic testing, and multidisciplinary tumor board reviews — add time before surgery begins. Prior authorization requirements from insurers create additional bottlenecks.

The COVID-19 pandemic made things worse. Elective surgeries were paused for months in 2020, and the resulting backlog cascaded through healthcare systems for years. Though most hospitals have cleared their pandemic-era backlogs, baseline wait times have not returned to pre-2020 levels in many regions.

Disparities Persist Across Race and Geography

The study's findings on disparities echo years of previous research. Black patients with breast cancer wait a median of 34-37 days for surgery, compared to 28-29 days for white patients. Patients at community hospitals, those in the most deprived areas, and those navigating complex referral pathways face disproportionately long delays.

These gaps matter because delayed treatment does not affect all groups equally. The same populations that face the longest waits also tend to present with more advanced disease and have fewer resources to navigate the healthcare system.

What Can Be Done

Health systems are experimenting with solutions. Some cancer centers have implemented digital scheduling tools and operational simulations to identify bottlenecks. Rutgers Cancer Institute, for example, used a digital twin model to cut its lab turnaround times from 90 minutes to under 30, nearly doubling the number of infusion patients it treats daily.

Researchers say the findings should inform policy at the system level — from insurance reform to surgical capacity planning — to ensure that the time between a cancer diagnosis and the first treatment does not continue to grow.
